task: Wave 12 read-only source preparation, making lane
scope: Three prospective bounded cases, no repository writes; production years are not invention or global first dates.

cases.ready: conditional: yes with explicitly broad, disputed phase dating
cases.capability: Moche workshop mould-making and mould-based ceramic production, supported by matrices, moulds, clay, unfired objects and firing remains rather than one museum vessel.
cases.why_distinct: Current records cover early fired vessels, wheel throwing, and Tang painted ware; this is a repeatable mould-creation and mould-forming workflow, not merely another vessel.
cases.witness_date: The fineware workshop occupies three Moche IV floors. One archaeological synthesis places Moche IV artefact circulation approximately 400–850 CE; this contextual chronology is not a direct date for each mould. The older fineware workshop and newly excavated CA-60 are distinct contexts. Check competing chronologies before assigning precise event bounds.

sources.locator: Huacas de Moche workshops, especially para. on more than 1,000 moulds and three Moche IV floors; household comparison
sources.supports: Fineware workshop has >1,000 moulds reported alongside production tools, unfired work and three stratified floors; material distribution and social organization involve interpretation, not proven exclusive elite ownership.
Moche IV artefacts circulated at the site approximately 400–850 CE, a broad contextual bound rather than direct dating of the workshop.
Mould-made decorated vessels appear in domestic and ritual settings as well as burials; function and access varied.

sources.type: original archaeological article; indexed abstract and sampled sections inspected, direct full text returned 403
sources.locator: Abstract, introduction and 167-mould sample from CA-60 room 60-11
sources.supports: A separate workshop sample exhibits variation in mould-making; 167 is the analysed sample, not all workshop production, and inferred artisan autonomy/elite oversight remains interpretation.

transfer_and_access_questions: Which directly dated samples or linked stratigraphy constrain the specific older workshop floors?
Which finished household objects are demonstrably matched to workshop moulds?
What evidence supports patronage, remuneration or differential access, beyond archaeological interpretation?
Mould use is not by itself evidence of mass output, cost reduction or transmission across regions.

cases.ready: yes for the 1817 observed loom, with 1819 publication distinguished
cases.capability: Asante weavers used narrow strips on a foot-operated loom and joined bands into larger cloth; silk threads from imported cloth were reworked locally.
cases.why_distinct: Existing Egyptian flax-weaving record does not document this foot-loom and joined narrow-strip production configuration or its observed imported-fibre supply pathway.
cases.witness_date: Bowdich visited Kumase in 1817 and published his observations in 1819; do not date the later Met specimen ca. 1910–1940 to 1817, or assert that all elements of a modern description apply to the earlier loom.

sources.locator: Textiles and Dyes excerpt, attributed to Mission from Cape Coast Castle to Ashantee (1819)
sources.supports: Describes an Asante loom actuated by toe-controlled strings, cloth not exceeding four inches wide, and unravelling silk for local weaving; colonial observer account, not an invention date.

sources.locator: Weaving and trade, pages describing Bowdich visit
sources.supports: Dates Bowdich’s direct Kumase observation to 1817, describes the donated loom, and discusses northern and neighbouring influences as possibilities, not proven pathways.

Dates a separate Asante silk example to circa 1910–1940; explains narrow double-heddle strips joined together, royal control, labor and expensive inputs. These details are not all directly dated to the 1817 witness.

transfer_and_access_questions: What does Bowdich directly record on silk supply, production costs and distribution?
Who had access to court-controlled cloth, and which named makers or workshop communities are documented?
Track neighbouring influences as questions rather than inferring a direct loan from similarity.

cases.ready: yes for the January 1901 written description; the workshop photograph purchased in 1900 provides a terminus ante quem for that image, not an exact production date
cases.capability: Women artisans used a spouted canting to apply wax resist for patterned cloth; separate subsequent colour application is described by museum sources.
cases.why_distinct: Wax-resist image registration changes dye uptake and is a different manufacturing operation from existing woven linen, bast cloth and Maya Blue mineral pigment.
cases.witness_date: A museum catalogue quotes a January 1901 letter describing the process and reproduces a Java workshop photo acquired in 1900; RISD describes a separate 19th-century wax-resist cloth. Do not turn either into an origin date or infer workshop identity from the photo purchase alone.

sources.type: museum catalogue with reproduced contemporary letter, inspected excerpt
sources.supports: A January 1901 letter reports Javanese women applying wax with canting tools; catalogue caption identifies a workshop photo bought in Java in 1900. The text is an outsider’s account and does not name the artisans.
A separate Javanese cotton wrapper dated to the 1800s is identified as wax-resist-dyed; the source associates some styles with court status.
Describes wax as a dye barrier and differentiates hand-drawn from stamped processes. Modern process description does not independently date ancient practice.

transfer_and_access_questions: What local-language or practitioner sources name the artisans and document workshop pay, capital and access to cloth and dyes?
Which evidence establishes when stamp-applied resist became commercially accessible, without transferring modern details into earlier witnesses?
Do not claim Java originated all wax resist or assume direct relation to Yoruba starch-resist.

alternative_not_selected.finding: Met catalogue identifies a Yoruba adire eleko wrapper signed Olebabehn, cassava-starch resist and indigo, and states collected at Oje market, Ibadan, in 1971. It assigns the object to the first half of the 20th century, while another scholarly caption says the production date is unknown; the British Museum object page was inaccessible (403). Use 1971 collection only as a bound if the date issue cannot be resolved.
